text: Sir William Ramsay KCB FRS FRSE (/ˈræmzi/; 2 October 1852 – 23 July 1916) was a Scottish chemist who discovered the noble gases and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1904 "in recognition of his services in the discovery of the inert gaseous elements in air" alongside John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh, who received the Nobel Prize in Physics that same year for their discovery of argon. After identifying argon, Ramsay investigated other atmospheric gases, isolating argon, helium, neon, krypton, and xenon, which led to the creation of a new section of the periodic table. Born on 2 October 1852 at 2 Clifton Street in Glasgow, the son of civil engineer William C. Ramsay and Catherine Robertson, he lived in a three-storey and basement Georgian townhouse at 2 Clifton Street before moving to 1 Oakvale Place in Hillhead as a youth. He was a nephew of geologist Sir Andrew Ramsay. Educated at Glasgow Academy, he apprenticed with Robert Napier in Govan before studying chemistry at the University of Glasgow, matriculating in 1866 and graduating in 1869. He then trained with chemist Thomas Anderson and studied in Germany at the University of Tübingen under Wilhelm Rudolph Fittig, completing a doctoral thesis on Investigations in the Toluic and Nitrotoluic Acids. He returned to Glasgow as Anderson's assistant and was appointed Professor of Chemistry at University College of Bristol in 1879, marrying Margaret Buchanan in 1881 and becoming Principal of the college that same year while conducting active research in organic chemistry and gases. In 1876, he synthesized pyridine from acetylene and hydrogen cyanide in an iron-tube furnace, marking the first synthesis of a heteroaromatic compound. In 1887, he succeeded Alexander Williamson as chair of Chemistry at University College London (UCL), where he made his most significant discoveries. As early as 1885–1890, he published notable papers on nitrogen oxides. On 19 April 1894, after attending a lecture by Lord Rayleigh, who had observed a discrepancy in nitrogen density, Ramsay and Rayleigh began investigating the issue. In August 1894, Ramsay informed Rayleigh of a new, heavy, chemically inert component of air, which he named argon from the Greek word meaning "lazy." In subsequent years, working with Morris Travers, he discovered neon, krypton, and xenon. He also isolated helium, previously only observed in the sun's spectrum, and in 1910 isolated and characterized radon. Between 1893 and 1902, he collaborated with British chemist Emily Aston on mineral analysis and atomic weight determination, including studies on the molecular surface energies of mixtures of non-associating liquids. He was elected an International Member of the American Philosophical Society in 1899 and an International Member of the United States National Academy of Sciences in 1904. In 1902, he was appointed a Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath (KCB) in the Coronation Honours list, invested by King Edward VII at Buckingham Palace on 24 October 1902. Ramsay served as president of the British Association from 1911 to 1912. He married Margaret Johnstone Marshall (née Buchanan) in 1881; they had a daughter, Catherine Elizabeth (Elska), and a son, William George, who died at age 40. He lived in Hazlemere, Buckinghamshire, and died in High Wycombe on 23 July 1916 at the age of 63 from nasal cancer and was buried in Hazlemere parish church. A blue plaque at 12 Arundel Gardens, Notting Hill, commemorates his life and work. The Sir William Ramsay School in Hazlemere and Ramsay grease are named after him. A memorial to him is located in the north aisle of the choir at Westminster Abbey by Charles Hartwell. In 1923, University College London named its Chemical Engineering department and seat after Ramsay, funded by the Ramsay Memorial Fund, with H. E. Watson, one of his former graduates, serving as the third Ramsay professor of chemical engineering. On 2 October 2019, Google celebrated his 167th birthday with a Google Doodle.
